# Debug Journal — final gate Chrome shutdown timeout
Started: 2026-08-16T15:10:00+09:00
Goal: Classify and resolve the final-gate Chrome process exit timeout without hiding a flake.

## Environment snapshot
- Runtime: Bun 1.3.14 test runner; Node 26.3.1 browser harness; Playwright Core 1.62.1; Chrome stable.
- Entry: `bun run check`; failing test `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`.
- Concurrent work at failure: two Vite dev servers, ingestion pytest, two visual-QA browser reviewers.
- Git HEAD: `ae0f05f`.
- References read: debugging runtime/node, methodology 00-setup, 03-flaky-triage, 02-investigate.

## Hypotheses
1. [OPEN] Concurrent browser/test workloads starved cleanup long enough to hit the 30s Chrome exit deadline. Distinguishing evidence: failing test passes alone after all background QA and dev servers stop. If true, fix is: quiet rerun.
2. [OPEN] A Chrome process/profile leaked from our manual QA and interfered with harness-owned process cleanup. Distinguishing evidence: process listing shows Chrome outside the active Bun harness tree before isolated repro. If true, fix is: cleanup ownership.
3. [OPEN] The harness has a deterministic Node 26/Chrome shutdown regression independent of contention. Distinguishing evidence: same exit timeout repeats in isolated test on a quiet machine. If true, fix is: harness teardown.
4. [CONFIRMED] Ingestion suite invocation omitted `.venv/Scripts` from PATH, so `shutil.which("impromptu-ingestion")` returned None. Distinguishing evidence: 84 tests passed and only the installed-executable lookup failed. If true, fix is: PATH invocation.

## Failed hypothesis round counter
- Round 1: full quiet suite moved the failure from WP3 to WP4; both files pass alone.
- Round 2: pending exact browser-E2E sequence reproduction.

## Artifacts to revert
- [ ] `.debug-journal.md` — remove after classification and final verification.
- [ ] `.git/info/exclude` entry for `.debug-journal.md` — remove after cleanup.
- [ ] `%TEMP%/impromptu-browser-sequence.log` — remove after classification.

## Findings
- `bun run check`: `Chrome process exit timeout` at prepared-evidence.harness.ts:975.
- ingestion pytest: `shutil.which("impromptu-ingestion") is None`; 84 passed, 1 failed.
- Quiet preflight after stopping Vite and parallel QA: `RELEVANT_COUNT=0`.
- Isolated `bun test tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`: 1 passed in 30.47s.
- Ingestion with `.venv/Scripts` on PATH: 85 passed in 27.84s.
- Quiet full suite: WP3 passed in 23.35s, but WP4 failed after 142.04s.
- Isolated WP4: 1 passed in 65.84s; no topology/Chrome process or port remained afterward.

## Final fix
- No product change required. H1 confirmed as concurrent-run resource contention; H2 and H3
  refuted by a clean process inventory and the isolated green run. Re-run the full gate only
  after stopping browser/dev/pytest workloads.

find .omo/senpi-task -maxdepth 8 -type f -printf '%p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort | head -500

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command '$t=[IO.Path]::GetTempPath(); Write-Output $t; $p=Join-Path $t "impromptu-browser-sequence.log"; if(Test-Path $p){Get-Item $p | Format-List FullName,Length,LastWriteTime; Get-Content $p}else{"NO_SEQUENCE_LOG"}'

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command 'Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object {$_.Name -in @("chrome.exe","node.exe","bun.exe")} | Select-Object Name,ProcessId,ParentProcessId,CreationDate,CommandLine | Format-List'

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command '$t=[IO.Path]::GetTempPath(); Get-ChildItem $t -Filter *.log -File | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 100 FullName,Length,LastWriteTime | Format-Table -AutoSize'

powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command '$t=[IO.Path]::GetTempPath(); Get-ChildItem $t -Filter *.log -File | Select-String -Pattern "Chrome process exit timeout|WP4 Windows topology|142.04|did not occur within|projection fixture rejected|TimeoutError" -SimpleMatch:$false | Select-Object Path,LineNumber,Line | Format-List'

## Conclusion

The exact full-suite root cause is **inconclusive** because WP4’s failure assertion was unavailable. I found no persistent profile, service-worker, port, or Chrome leak that explains both failures.

The strongest explanation is **resource/handle accumulation in the long-lived, non-isolated Bun test process combined with fragile browser teardown deadlines**. The browser harnesses themselves already run in fresh Node subprocesses, so isolating their Bun wrapper files from the other 67 files is the lowest-risk deterministic fix.

## Concrete findings

- `package.json:23` runs all 69 files in one Bun process without `--isolate`.
- Bun 1.3.14 explicitly provides `--isolate` so leaked globals and handles from one test file cannot affect another.

Specific cleanup defects can accumulate before the browser gates:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` and `:192` open SSE response bodies but never consume or cancel them. Service processes are killed in `afterEach`, but the parent-side fetch streams are not explicitly released.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls asynchronous `server.stop(true)` without awaiting it.
- Several successful waits create uncancellable `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers. Most are bounded to 2–10 seconds, so they are real transient retention rather than a convincing multi-minute root cause:
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`
  - `apps/stage/src/App.test.tsx:57,70`

WP3 teardown has a more serious failure-path flaw:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-984` waits only five seconds for natural Chrome exit.
- If that deadline expires at `:975`, execution skips service termination and profile cleanup at `:984-987`.
- Thus the reported “Chrome process exit timeout” is primarily a brittle cleanup assertion; once triggered, it also creates an actual process/resource leak.
- CDP disconnect and OS process exit are separate events. Under complete-suite pressure, Chrome can disconnect correctly but take over five seconds for its process tree to terminate.

WP4’s harness is cleaner:

- It uses Playwright-owned `chromium.launch()` and `browser.close()` at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:888`.
- Its module-level `process.on("unhandledRejection")` at `:3` is never removed, but this module runs in a one-shot Node subprocess, so it cannot accumulate across the 69 Bun files.
- Profiles and service workers are not shared: WP3 uses a PID-qualified clean profile; WP4 uses ephemeral browser contexts.

Happy DOM is not the primary leak:

- Registrations in the React tests pair `GlobalRegistrator.register()` with an awaited Promise-returning `afterAll(() => GlobalRegistrator.unregister())`.
- `tests/setup.ts` is no longer a Bun preload; it is imported only by `UpdateCoordinator.test.ts`.
- Some tests leave window listeners attached, but unregistering Happy DOM closes that window after the file.

## Lowest-risk deterministic change

Split the heavyweight browser wrappers into fresh Bun invocations:

1. Run the ordinary suite while excluding:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Run WP3 in a fresh Bun process.
3. Run WP4 in another fresh Bun process.

This preserves every assertion, remains sequential, and introduces no sleeps, retries, skips, or weaker deadlines. It is stronger than merely adding `--isolate`, because each browser gate receives a fresh OS process and heap.

Secondarily, harden WP3 cleanup by using Playwright-owned `launchPersistentContext()` or by force-terminating and awaiting the Chrome process tree after CDP shutdown instead of failing before the remaining cleanup executes.

## Inspection performed

## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). ## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). Default configstore is `FileConfigstore` ([index.ts#L32-L46](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L32-L46)), which is just `FileKvStore` re-exported ([configstores/index.ts](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/configstores/index.ts)) — it writes `<id>.json` next to the upload: `await fs.writeFile(this.resolve(key), JSON.stringify(value))` ([FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12), [FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31)).
- **Write (PATCH)**: opens the same file with `fs.createWriteStream(file_path, { flags: 'r+', start: offset })` — appends at the exact client-reported offset — counts bytes through a transform, and returns the new `offset + bytes_received` ([index.ts#L97-L128](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L97-L128)).
- **Read (HEAD/resume)**: `getUpload` does NOT trust any in-memory counter. It re-reads the JSON info file for `size`/`metadata`/`creation_date` and then **`offset: stats.size`** — the actual byte length from `fs.stat` ([index.ts#L130-L165](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L130-L165)). So the source of truth for the resume offset is the persisted file itself; a process restart loses nothing.
- This "file + adjacent info file" layout is documented as the universal store pattern: *"All stores (as in the `datastore` option) save two files, the uploaded file and an info file with metadata, usually adjacent to each other"* ([server README, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).

### Where memory is used (and isn't)

- The default **locker** is `MemoryLocker` — `locks = new Map<string, LockEntry>()` in-process ([MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/lockers/MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34)); README says explicitly: *"By default it uses an in-memory locker... When running multiple instances of the server, you need to provide a locker implementation that is shared between all instances (such as a `RedisLocker`)"* ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- In-memory KV stores (`MemoryKvStore`, re-exported as `MemoryConfigstore`) exist but are intended as caches for cloud stores (e.g. `@tus/s3-store` `cache:` option) — the README's KV-store section only shows `MemoryKvStore` used as an S3 metadata cache, never as the source of truth ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- Conclusion for the report: **persisted** for FileStore (offset = file size on disk, metadata = JSON sidecar); **in-memory only** for the default lock and for optional cloud-store caches.

Evidence of Bun fitness:

- Its HTTP layer dependency `srvx ~0.11.15` ships a **first-class Bun adapter**: exports map has a `"bun"` condition → `./dist/adapters/bun.mjs`, plus a maintained `test:node-compat:bun` suite ([srvx 0.11.15 npm metadata](https://registry.npmjs.org/srvx/0.11.15)).
- `@tus/server` exposes two integration surfaces ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)):

  - `server.handleWeb(req: Request)` — web-standard only; documented for meta-frameworks and "a Node.js compatible runtime based on the web `Request` and `Response` API" (Next.js app-router example binds `GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE/OPTIONS/HEAD` to it). This is the natural fit for `Bun.serve({ fetch })`.

Minimal Bun snippet (shape taken from the pinned README's Next.js app-router example, adapted to `Bun.serve`):

```ts
import { Server } from "@tus/server";
import { FileStore } from "@tus/file-store";

const tusServer = new Server({
  path: "/files",
  datastore: new FileStore({ directory: "./uploads" }),
});

Bun.serve({ fetch: (req) => tusServer.handleWeb(req) });
```

What "minimal" additionally requires, from source:

1. **Don't let a framework body-parser consume PATCH bodies** — the raw `application/offset+octet-stream` stream must reach the store (README Fastify example adds a no-op content-type parser for exactly this reason). With `Bun.serve` + `handleWeb` the body stays intact.
2. **FileStore internals are all Bun-supported**: `node:fs`, `node:fs/promises`, `node:stream`, `stream/promises.pipeline` ([file-store index.ts imports](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L1-L7)).

4. **Single-process assumption**: default `MemoryLocker` is fine for the demo scale (~10 concurrent users, one process); horizontal scaling requires `RedisLocker`/`RedisKvStore` (optional deps `ioredis` / `@redis/client`).
5. **Durability coupling**: since offset = on-disk file size, the upload directory must be local/durable; a network FS would undermine the resume contract.

## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). ## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). Default configstore is `FileConfigstore` ([index.ts#L32-L46](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L32-L46)), which is just `FileKvStore` re-exported ([configstores/index.ts](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/configstores/index.ts)) — it writes `<id>.json` next to the upload: `await fs.writeFile(this.resolve(key), JSON.stringify(value))` ([FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12), [FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31)).
- **Write (PATCH)**: opens the same file with `fs.createWriteStream(file_path, { flags: 'r+', start: offset })` — appends at the exact client-reported offset — counts bytes through a transform, and returns the new `offset + bytes_received` ([index.ts#L97-L128](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L97-L128)).
- **Read (HEAD/resume)**: `getUpload` does NOT trust any in-memory counter. It re-reads the JSON info file for `size`/`metadata`/`creation_date` and then **`offset: stats.size`** — the actual byte length from `fs.stat` ([index.ts#L130-L165](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L130-L165)). So the source of truth for the resume offset is the persisted file itself; a process restart loses nothing.
- This "file + adjacent info file" layout is documented as the universal store pattern: *"All stores (as in the `datastore` option) save two files, the uploaded file and an info file with metadata, usually adjacent to each other"* ([server README, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).

### Where memory is used (and isn't)

- The default **locker** is `MemoryLocker` — `locks = new Map<string, LockEntry>()` in-process ([MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/lockers/MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34)); README says explicitly: *"By default it uses an in-memory locker... When running multiple instances of the server, you need to provide a locker implementation that is shared between all instances (such as a `RedisLocker`)"* ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- In-memory KV stores (`MemoryKvStore`, re-exported as `MemoryConfigstore`) exist but are intended as caches for cloud stores (e.g. `@tus/s3-store` `cache:` option) — the README's KV-store section only shows `MemoryKvStore` used as an S3 metadata cache, never as the source of truth ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- Conclusion for the report: **persisted** for FileStore (offset = file size on disk, metadata = JSON sidecar); **in-memory only** for the default lock and for optional cloud-store caches.

## Minimal Bun/TypeScript-compatible integration

Evidence of Bun fitness:

- `@tus/server` is pure ESM with bundled types (`"type": "module"`, `"types": "./dist/index.d.ts"`, `"exports": "./dist/index.js"`), engines `node >=20.19.0`; `@tus/file-store` same shape ([npm metadata](https://registry.npmjs.org/@tus/server/latest), [@tus/file-store](https://registry.npmjs.org/@tus/file-store/latest)). Workspace runs `bun@1.3.14`, so Node 20+ compatibility is satisfied.
- Its HTTP layer dependency `srvx ~0.11.15` ships a **first-class Bun adapter**: exports map has a `"bun"` condition → `./dist/adapters/bun.mjs`, plus a maintained `test:node-compat:bun` suite ([srvx 0.11.15 npm metadata](https://registry.npmjs.org/srvx/0.11.15)).
- `@tus/server` exposes two integration surfaces ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)):
  - `server.handle(req: http.IncomingMessage, res: http.ServerResponse)` — Node-idiomatic; converts to/from web `Request`/`Response` internally (Express/Koa/Fastify/Next pages-router examples).
  - `server.handleWeb(req: Request)` — web-standard only; documented for meta-frameworks and "a Node.js compatible runtime based on the web `Request` and `Response` API" (Next.js app-router example binds `GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE/OPTIONS/HEAD` to it). This is the natural fit for `Bun.serve({ fetch })`.

Minimal Bun snippet (shape taken from the pinned README's Next.js app-router example, adapted to `Bun.serve`):

```ts
import { Server } from "@tus/server";
import { FileStore } from "@tus/file-store";

const tusServer = new Server({
  path: "/files",
  datastore: new FileStore({ directory: "./uploads" }),
});

Bun.serve({ fetch: (req) => tusServer.handleWeb(req) });
```

What "minimal" additionally requires, from source:

1. **Don't let a framework body-parser consume PATCH bodies** — the raw `application/offset+octet-stream` stream must reach the store (README Fastify example adds a no-op content-type parser for exactly this reason). With `Bun.serve` + `handleWeb` the body stays intact.
2. **FileStore internals are all Bun-supported**: `node:fs`, `node:fs/promises`, `node:stream`, `stream/promises.pipeline` ([file-store index.ts imports](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L1-L7)).
3. **Known wart**: `checkOrCreateDirectory()` is fire-and-forget from the constructor (`// TODO: this async call can not happen in the constructor`, [index.ts#L44-L45](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L44-L45)) — pre-create the directory before first request.
4. **Single-process assumption**: default `MemoryLocker` is fine for the demo scale (~10 concurrent users, one process); horizontal scaling requires `RedisLocker`/`RedisKvStore` (optional deps `ioredis` / `@redis/client`).
5. **Durability coupling**: since offset = on-disk file size, the upload directory must be local/durable; a network FS would undermine the resume contract.
6. Path traversal is guarded (`isPathInsideDirectory` in `resolve()`), and `namingFunction`/`generateUrl`/`getFileIdFromRequest` are available if you want structured IDs ([index.ts#L59-L65](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L59-L65), [server README options](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
7. Client side would use `tus-js-client` (canonical JS client) — not deep-dived in this pass; its HEAD pin is available on request.

**Turn Context (split turn):**

## Original Request
Perform a read-only, evidence-based investigation of nondeterministic full-suite Bun failures affecting WP3/WP4 real-browser E2Es. Evaluate teardown exceptions, retained Bun resources, memory/GC pressure, test-order/global interference, and other mechanisms; inspect every browser lifecycle; provide exact lines, a falsifiable diagnosis, and the smallest deterministic test/fix plan without weakening thresholds or extending timeouts.

## Early Progress
- Confirmed `bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000` uses one shared Bun process unless `--isolate` is added.
- Located the real-browser paths:
  - WP3 test spawns a fresh Node verifier, which manually spawns Chrome and connects over CDP.
  - WP4 test spawns a fresh Node verifier using `chromium.launch`.
  - `scripts/verify-browser-runtime.ts` uses persistent Playwright contexts, but runs after the Bun suite as a separate command.
- Found a definite WP3 teardown defect around `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:949-985`: sequential cleanup awaits can throw at the Chrome exit wait (`~967-978`), skipping service termination and temporary-file/profile removal. Existing Windows process teardown helpers use bounded graceful shutdown plus `taskkill /t /f`, but WP3’s special Chrome path does not reuse that fallback.
- Found the analogous structural risk in WP4 around `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:887-893`: if `browser.close()` rejects/hangs, subsequent fixture/server cleanup is skipped. Context cleanup is likewise a single throwing await at lines `466-467` and `764-765`.
- Confirmed WP3/WP4 harness code executes in fresh Node children, so Bun module globals and Bun GC cannot directly mutate their JS heaps. Shared OS resources, inherited environment, filesystem state, parent memory pressure, or leaked children remain possible.
- Found no direct evidence yet that accumulated GC explains the failures. WP4 measures recovery with `performance.now()` and has 30-second event/recovery gates, but its exact 142-second failure is unavailable.
- The isolated sequence log confirms WP3 → realtime soak → WP4 passed in 116.05s. Full discovery order additionally includes `runtime-routes.test.ts` between the soak and WP4, so the reported reproducer was not the exact full-suite predecessor sequence.
- Reviewed shared-process candidates including Happy DOM global registration, AbortSignal timers/listeners, Bun servers, WebSockets, and spawned services. Most DOM-heavy tests occur after the E2Es, reducing their relevance to WP3/WP4; investigation of earlier retained handles was still ongoing.
- No files were modified.

## Context for Suffix
- Strongest established source fact: teardown is not exception-safe in both browser harnesses, and WP3’s observed timeout can deterministically skip all remaining cleanup.
- This defect explains leaked resources after a failure but does not alone explain why the initial Chrome close times out or the separate WP4 142-second failure.
- Key remaining work is to inspect the missing `runtime-routes` predecessor and all earlier Bun-side servers/handles, determine whether any survive cleanup, and distinguish shared-parent interference using `--isolate` or an exact-order targeted run.
- Relevant locations:
  - WP3 browser launch/cleanup: `prepared-evidence.harness.ts` around `473` and `949-985`.
  - WP4 waits/thresholds: `windows-topology.harness.ts:262-304`, `596-602`.
  - WP4 launch/cleanup: `windows-topology.harness.ts:769-798`, `887-893`.
  - Realtime soak cleanup: `realtime-soak.harness.ts:614-616`.
  - Bun subprocess cleanup examples: `runtime-routes.test.ts` and `durable-main-restart.test.ts`.

# Debug Journal — final gate Chrome shutdown timeout
Started: 2026-08-16T15:10:00+09:00
Goal: Classify and resolve the final-gate Chrome process exit timeout without hiding a flake.

## Environment snapshot
- Runtime: Bun 1.3.14 test runner; Node 26.3.1 browser harness; Playwright Core 1.62.1; Chrome stable.
- Entry: `bun run check`; failing test `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`.
- Concurrent work at failure: two Vite dev servers, ingestion pytest, two visual-QA browser reviewers.
- Git HEAD: `ae0f05f`.
- References read: debugging runtime/node, methodology 00-setup, 03-flaky-triage, 02-investigate.

## Hypotheses
1. [OPEN] Concurrent browser/test workloads starved cleanup long enough to hit the 30s Chrome exit deadline. Distinguishing evidence: failing test passes alone after all background QA and dev servers stop. If true, fix is: quiet rerun.
2. [OPEN] A Chrome process/profile leaked from our manual QA and interfered with harness-owned process cleanup. Distinguishing evidence: process listing shows Chrome outside the active Bun harness tree before isolated repro. If true, fix is: cleanup ownership.
3. [OPEN] The harness has a deterministic Node 26/Chrome shutdown regression independent of contention. Distinguishing evidence: same exit timeout repeats in isolated test on a quiet machine. If true, fix is: harness teardown.
4. [CONFIRMED] Ingestion suite invocation omitted `.venv/Scripts` from PATH, so `shutil.which("impromptu-ingestion")` returned None. Distinguishing evidence: 84 tests passed and only the installed-executable lookup failed. If true, fix is: PATH invocation.

## Failed hypothesis round counter
- Round 1: full quiet suite moved the failure from WP3 to WP4; both files pass alone.
- Round 2: pending exact browser-E2E sequence reproduction.

## Artifacts to revert
- [ ] `.debug-journal.md` — remove after classification and final verification.
- [ ] `.git/info/exclude` entry for `.debug-journal.md` — remove after cleanup.
- [ ] `%TEMP%/impromptu-browser-sequence.log` — remove after classification.

## Findings
- `bun run check`: `Chrome process exit timeout` at prepared-evidence.harness.ts:975.
- ingestion pytest: `shutil.which("impromptu-ingestion") is None`; 84 passed, 1 failed.
- Quiet preflight after stopping Vite and parallel QA: `RELEVANT_COUNT=0`.
- Isolated `bun test tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`: 1 passed in 30.47s.
- Ingestion with `.venv/Scripts` on PATH: 85 passed in 27.84s.
- Quiet full suite: WP3 passed in 23.35s, but WP4 failed after 142.04s.
- Isolated WP4: 1 passed in 65.84s; no topology/Chrome process or port remained afterward.
- Exact WP3 -> realtime-soak -> WP4 process: 3 passed in 116.05s.
- While three analysis agents consumed CPU, an attempted `--list-tests` invocation actually ran
  the 67-file non-browser remainder (Bun 1.3.14 ignored listing intent) and produced four
  deadline-sensitive failures. Do not use that invocation as a product verdict; it confirms
  host contention materially changes the suite outcome.

## Final fix
- Split the 67-file shared-runner suite and both real-browser wrappers into three sequential
  Bun invocations. Every assertion remains enabled, but WP3 and WP4 now start with a fresh OS
  process/heap instead of inheriting accumulated handles and host pressure from earlier files.
- H1 confirmed as shared-runner/host resource contention. Persistent browser/profile leaks and
  direct WP3 -> WP4 contamination were refuted by clean process inventories, isolated green
  runs, and the exact three-test sequence passing.

WP3 first closes the context and sends `Browser.close`:

It then allows only five seconds for OS process exit:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:967-979`

If that deadline expires at `:975`, the exception aborts the `finally` block before:

- Remaining services are terminated: `:984`

Therefore, `Chrome process exit timeout` does not establish a failed browser scenario. It says the E2E completed but Chrome did not finish OS-level teardown within five seconds. Under resource pressure, the cleanup assertion becomes the test failure and creates the leak it was intended to detect.

## Concrete findings

- `package.json:23` runs all 69 files in one Bun process without `--isolate`.
- Bun 1.3.14 explicitly provides `--isolate` so leaked globals and handles from one test file cannot affect another.

Specific cleanup defects can accumulate before the browser gates:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` and `:192` open SSE response bodies but never consume or cancel them. Service processes are killed in `afterEach`, but the parent-side fetch streams are not explicitly released.

  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`

- CDP disconnect and OS process exit are separate events. Under complete-suite pressure, Chrome can disconnect correctly but take over five seconds for its process tree to terminate.

WP4’s harness is cleaner:

- It uses Playwright-owned `chromium.launch()` and `browser.close()` at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:888`.

- `tests/setup.ts` is no longer a Bun preload; it is imported only by `UpdateCoordinator.test.ts`.

result:"I read this as a read-only root-cause review - I traced the shared Bun runner, subprocess boundaries, browser ownership, and earlier service lifecycle, then ranked the evidence and selected the smallest isolation fix.

## ROOT CAUSE

### 1. Most likely: long-lived Bun-suite resource/handle accumulation reaches timing-sensitive browser subprocesses

The browser behavior itself is not sequence-dependent:

- WP3 passes alone.
- WP4 passes alone.
- The exact WP3 -> soak -> WP4 sequence passes.
- The failing browser alternates between full runs.

That rules against shared browser profiles, fixed E2E ordering, and direct WP3-to-WP4 contamination. The material difference is the preceding 66 test files sharing one Bun process.

Architecture:

1. `package.json:23` runs every test file in one non-isolated Bun invocation.
2. WP3 and WP4 wrappers spawn one-shot Node verifiers:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts:41`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts:50`
3. Those Node processes own Chrome and services; earlier test modules cannot directly mutate their module state. They can, however, leave the Bun parent with memory, timers, streams, sockets, or OS pressure while it waits for them.

WP4 is explicitly wall-clock sensitive:

- Event waits default to 30 seconds: `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:265`
- Recovery duration uses `performance.now()`: `:596-601`
- Any recovery over 30 seconds becomes a gate failure: `:602`
- The verifier rejects the aggregate: `scripts/verify-wp4-topology-e2e.ts:11-18`

Normal WP4 took 65.84 seconds; failed WP4 took 142.04 seconds. The additional approximately 76 seconds is consistent with delayed browser/event processing or multiple recovery deadlines, not deterministic state corruption.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The missing WP4 assertion prevents proving whether it was a recovery deadline, event timeout, or teardown failure.

### 2. Confirmed amplifier: WP3 cleanup turns delayed Chrome exit into a failure and then skips all remaining cleanup

WP3 first closes the context and sends `Browser.close`:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-958`

It then allows only five seconds for OS process exit:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:967-979`

If that deadline expires at `:975`, the exception aborts the `finally` block before:

- Remaining services are terminated: `:984`
- Profile and snapshots are removed: `:985-987`

Therefore, `Chrome process exit timeout` does not establish a failed browser scenario. It says the E2E completed but Chrome did not finish OS-level teardown within five seconds. Under resource pressure, the cleanup assertion becomes the test failure and creates the leak it was intended to detect.

WP3 also launches bare Chrome manually with a persistent profile and CDP port at `:471-488`, unlike WP4’s Playwright-owned launch at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:798`. That increases lifecycle code and shutdown states owned by the harness.

**Confidence: high for the reported WP3 failure and cleanup leak; it does not alone explain WP4.**

### 3. Lower-ranked contributor: earlier successful tests retain parent-side handles briefly

Concrete examples:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` opens an SSE response without consuming or cancelling its body.
- The same occurs for controller events at `:192`.
- Cleanup kills services at `:11-16`, but does not explicitly release those response bodies.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls `server.stop(true)` without awaiting completion.
- Several earlier tests leave bounded `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers alive after successful waits:
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`

These are real retention defects in a shared runner, but none individually explains a 142-second WP4 failure. They support isolation as the correct boundary rather than identifying one specific leaked timer as the cause.

## Ruled out

- **WP3 profile persistence:** profile is PID-qualified and deleted before startup: `prepared-evidence.harness.ts:371,380`.
- **WP4 service-worker/profile persistence:** it uses fresh Playwright contexts at `windows-topology.harness.ts:419,480`, closed at `:467,765`.
- **WP4 artifact persistence:** artifact root is removed at `:770`.
- **Environment mutation:** the test files only pass `Bun.env`; no test mutates relevant environment variables.
- **Module-scope port collision as the common cause:** WP3/WP4 allocate ephemeral ports, and the exact sequence succeeds.
- **Direct WP3 -> soak -> WP4 leak:** falsified by the supplied 116.05-second successful sequence.

## MINIMAL FIX — Recommended design

Run the two real-browser wrappers in separate Bun invocations after the ordinary suite.

Conceptually:

1. Run all tests except:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Start a fresh Bun process for WP3.
3. Start another fresh Bun process for WP4.

This retains every existing assertion and serial execution while discarding the ordinary suite’s heap, timers, streams, globals, and handles before each browser gate.

### Alternative design: add `--isolate`

Add `--isolate` to `package.json:23`.

Trade-offs:

- Smaller textual change.
- Addresses cross-file globals and leaked handles.
- Does not provide as strong an OS-process/heap boundary as separate invocations.
- Makes diagnosis harder because browser failures remain buried inside the 69-file run.

### Alternative design: browser-lifecycle refactor

Replace WP3’s manual Chrome spawn/CDP/process tracking with the existing Playwright `launchPersistentContext()` pattern used in `scripts/verify-browser-runtime.ts:400`.

Trade-offs:

- Removes duplicated Chrome lifecycle machinery and the remote-debugging-port allocation.
- Better direct fix for WP3 shutdown.
- Does not address the alternating WP4 full-suite failure.
- Higher migration risk than changing the test invocation boundary.

**Recommendation:** split the two wrappers into fresh invocations. Also harden WP3 teardown separately so a graceful-exit timeout escalates to Windows process-tree termination and cleanup continues. Do not extend timeouts or retry failed tests.

## Deterministic verification

After applying the split, run the ordinary prefix once and each browser gate three times in fresh processes:

```bash
mapfile -t core_tests < <(
  find apps packages scripts services tests -type f \
    \( -name '*.test.ts' -o -name '*.test.tsx' \) \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts' \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts' |
  sort
)

bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 "${core_tests[@]}" &&
for run in 1 2 3; do
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts &&
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts ||
  exit 1
done
```

This is repetition for verification, not a retry-based production fix. No files were modified and no additional full suite was run."

result:"I read this as a read-only root-cause review - I traced the shared Bun runner, subprocess boundaries, browser ownership, and earlier service lifecycle, then ranked the evidence and selected the smallest isolation fix.

## ROOT CAUSE

### 1. Most likely: long-lived Bun-suite resource/handle accumulation reaches timing-sensitive browser subprocesses

The browser behavior itself is not sequence-dependent:

- WP3 passes alone.
- WP4 passes alone.
- The exact WP3 -> soak -> WP4 sequence passes.
- The failing browser alternates between full runs.

That rules against shared browser profiles, fixed E2E ordering, and direct WP3-to-WP4 contamination. The material difference is the preceding 66 test files sharing one Bun process.

Architecture:

1. `package.json:23` runs every test file in one non-isolated Bun invocation.
2. WP3 and WP4 wrappers spawn one-shot Node verifiers:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts:41`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts:50`
3. Those Node processes own Chrome and services; earlier test modules cannot directly mutate their module state. They can, however, leave the Bun parent with memory, timers, streams, sockets, or OS pressure while it waits for them.

WP4 is explicitly wall-clock sensitive:

- Event waits default to 30 seconds: `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:265`
- Recovery duration uses `performance.now()`: `:596-601`
- Any recovery over 30 seconds becomes a gate failure: `:602`
- The verifier rejects the aggregate: `scripts/verify-wp4-topology-e2e.ts:11-18`

Normal WP4 took 65.84 seconds; failed WP4 took 142.04 seconds. The additional approximately 76 seconds is consistent with delayed browser/event processing or multiple recovery deadlines, not deterministic state corruption.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The missing WP4 assertion prevents proving whether it was a recovery deadline, event timeout, or teardown failure.

### 2. Confirmed amplifier: WP3 cleanup turns delayed Chrome exit into a failure and then skips all remaining cleanup

WP3 first closes the context and sends `Browser.close`:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-958`

It then allows only five seconds for OS process exit:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:967-979`

If that deadline expires at `:975`, the exception aborts the `finally` block before:

- Remaining services are terminated: `:984`
- Profile and snapshots are removed: `:985-987`

Therefore, `Chrome process exit timeout` does not establish a failed browser scenario. It says the E2E completed but Chrome did not finish OS-level teardown within five seconds. Under resource pressure, the cleanup assertion becomes the test failure and creates the leak it was intended to detect.

WP3 also launches bare Chrome manually with a persistent profile and CDP port at `:471-488`, unlike WP4’s Playwright-owned launch at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:798`. That increases lifecycle code and shutdown states owned by the harness.

**Confidence: high for the reported WP3 failure and cleanup leak; it does not alone explain WP4.**

### 3. Lower-ranked contributor: earlier successful tests retain parent-side handles briefly

Concrete examples:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` opens an SSE response without consuming or cancelling its body.
- The same occurs for controller events at `:192`.
- Cleanup kills services at `:11-16`, but does not explicitly release those response bodies.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls `server.stop(true)` without awaiting completion.
- Several earlier tests leave bounded `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers alive after successful waits:
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`

These are real retention defects in a shared runner, but none individually explains a 142-second WP4 failure. They support isolation as the correct boundary rather than identifying one specific leaked timer as the cause.

## Ruled out

- **WP3 profile persistence:** profile is PID-qualified and deleted before startup: `prepared-evidence.harness.ts:371,380`.
- **WP4 service-worker/profile persistence:** it uses fresh Playwright contexts at `windows-topology.harness.ts:419,480`, closed at `:467,765`.
- **WP4 artifact persistence:** artifact root is removed at `:770`.
- **Environment mutation:** the test files only pass `Bun.env`; no test mutates relevant environment variables.
- **Module-scope port collision as the common cause:** WP3/WP4 allocate ephemeral ports, and the exact sequence succeeds.
- **Direct WP3 -> soak -> WP4 leak:** falsified by the supplied 116.05-second successful sequence.

## MINIMAL FIX — Recommended design

Run the two real-browser wrappers in separate Bun invocations after the ordinary suite.

Conceptually:

1. Run all tests except:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Start a fresh Bun process for WP3.
3. Start another fresh Bun process for WP4.

This retains every existing assertion and serial execution while discarding the ordinary suite’s heap, timers, streams, globals, and handles before each browser gate.

### Alternative design: add `--isolate`

Add `--isolate` to `package.json:23`.

Trade-offs:

- Smaller textual change.
- Addresses cross-file globals and leaked handles.
- Does not provide as strong an OS-process/heap boundary as separate invocations.
- Makes diagnosis harder because browser failures remain buried inside the 69-file run.

### Alternative design: browser-lifecycle refactor

Replace WP3’s manual Chrome spawn/CDP/process tracking with the existing Playwright `launchPersistentContext()` pattern used in `scripts/verify-browser-runtime.ts:400`.

Trade-offs:

- Removes duplicated Chrome lifecycle machinery and the remote-debugging-port allocation.
- Better direct fix for WP3 shutdown.
- Does not address the alternating WP4 full-suite failure.
- Higher migration risk than changing the test invocation boundary.

**Recommendation:** split the two wrappers into fresh invocations. Also harden WP3 teardown separately so a graceful-exit timeout escalates to Windows process-tree termination and cleanup continues. Do not extend timeouts or retry failed tests.

## Deterministic verification

After applying the split, run the ordinary prefix once and each browser gate three times in fresh processes:

```bash
mapfile -t core_tests < <(
  find apps packages scripts services tests -type f \
    \( -name '*.test.ts' -o -name '*.test.tsx' \) \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts' \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts' |
  sort
)

bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 "${core_tests[@]}" &&
for run in 1 2 3; do
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts &&
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts ||
  exit 1
done
```

This is repetition for verification, not a retry-based production fix. No files were modified and no additional full suite was run."

- `package.json:23` runs all 69 files in one Bun process without `--isolate`.

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` and `:192` open SSE response bodies but never consume or cancel them. Service processes are killed in `afterEach`, but the parent-side fetch streams are not explicitly released.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls asynchronous `server.stop(true)` without awaiting it.
- Several successful waits create uncancellable `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers. Most are bounded to 2–10 seconds, so they are real transient retention rather than a convincing multi-minute root cause:
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`

- Registrations in the React tests pair `GlobalRegistrator.register()` with an awaited Promise-returning `afterAll(() => GlobalRegistrator.unregister())`.

Split the heavyweight browser wrappers into fresh Bun invocations:

1. Run the ordinary suite while excluding:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Run WP3 in a fresh Bun process.
3. Run WP4 in another fresh Bun process.

This preserves every assertion, remains sequential, and introduces no sleeps, retries, skips, or weaker deadlines. It is stronger than merely adding `--isolate`, because each browser gate receives a fresh OS process and heap.

Secondarily, harden WP3 cleanup by using Playwright-owned `launchPersistentContext()` or by force-terminating and awaiting the Chrome process tree after CDP shutdown instead of failing before the remaining cleanup executes.

result:"I read this as a read-only root-cause review - I traced the shared Bun runner, subprocess boundaries, browser ownership, and earlier service lifecycle, then ranked the evidence and selected the smallest isolation fix.

## ROOT CAUSE

### 1. Most likely: long-lived Bun-suite resource/handle accumulation reaches timing-sensitive browser subprocesses

The browser behavior itself is not sequence-dependent:

- WP3 passes alone.
- WP4 passes alone.
- The exact WP3 -> soak -> WP4 sequence passes.
- The failing browser alternates between full runs.

That rules against shared browser profiles, fixed E2E ordering, and direct WP3-to-WP4 contamination. The material difference is the preceding 66 test files sharing one Bun process.

Architecture:

1. `package.json:23` runs every test file in one non-isolated Bun invocation.
2. WP3 and WP4 wrappers spawn one-shot Node verifiers:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts:41`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts:50`
3. Those Node processes own Chrome and services; earlier test modules cannot directly mutate their module state. They can, however, leave the Bun parent with memory, timers, streams, sockets, or OS pressure while it waits for them.

WP4 is explicitly wall-clock sensitive:

- Event waits default to 30 seconds: `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:265`
- Recovery duration uses `performance.now()`: `:596-601`
- Any recovery over 30 seconds becomes a gate failure: `:602`
- The verifier rejects the aggregate: `scripts/verify-wp4-topology-e2e.ts:11-18`

Normal WP4 took 65.84 seconds; failed WP4 took 142.04 seconds. The additional approximately 76 seconds is consistent with delayed browser/event processing or multiple recovery deadlines, not deterministic state corruption.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The missing WP4 assertion prevents proving whether it was a recovery deadline, event timeout, or teardown failure.

### 2. Confirmed amplifier: WP3 cleanup turns delayed Chrome exit into a failure and then skips all remaining cleanup

WP3 first closes the context and sends `Browser.close`:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-958`

It then allows only five seconds for OS process exit:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:967-979`

If that deadline expires at `:975`, the exception aborts the `finally` block before:

- Remaining services are terminated: `:984`
- Profile and snapshots are removed: `:985-987`

Therefore, `Chrome process exit timeout` does not establish a failed browser scenario. It says the E2E completed but Chrome did not finish OS-level teardown within five seconds. Under resource pressure, the cleanup assertion becomes the test failure and creates the leak it was intended to detect.

WP3 also launches bare Chrome manually with a persistent profile and CDP port at `:471-488`, unlike WP4’s Playwright-owned launch at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:798`. That increases lifecycle code and shutdown states owned by the harness.

**Confidence: high for the reported WP3 failure and cleanup leak; it does not alone explain WP4.**

### 3. Lower-ranked contributor: earlier successful tests retain parent-side handles briefly

Concrete examples:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` opens an SSE response without consuming or cancelling its body.
- The same occurs for controller events at `:192`.
- Cleanup kills services at `:11-16`, but does not explicitly release those response bodies.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls `server.stop(true)` without awaiting completion.
- Several earlier tests leave bounded `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers alive after successful waits:
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`

These are real retention defects in a shared runner, but none individually explains a 142-second WP4 failure. They support isolation as the correct boundary rather than identifying one specific leaked timer as the cause.

## Ruled out

- **WP3 profile persistence:** profile is PID-qualified and deleted before startup: `prepared-evidence.harness.ts:371,380`.
- **WP4 service-worker/profile persistence:** it uses fresh Playwright contexts at `windows-topology.harness.ts:419,480`, closed at `:467,765`.
- **WP4 artifact persistence:** artifact root is removed at `:770`.
- **Environment mutation:** the test files only pass `Bun.env`; no test mutates relevant environment variables.
- **Module-scope port collision as the common cause:** WP3/WP4 allocate ephemeral ports, and the exact sequence succeeds.
- **Direct WP3 -> soak -> WP4 leak:** falsified by the supplied 116.05-second successful sequence.

## MINIMAL FIX — Recommended design

Run the two real-browser wrappers in separate Bun invocations after the ordinary suite.

Conceptually:

1. Run all tests except:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Start a fresh Bun process for WP3.
3. Start another fresh Bun process for WP4.

This retains every existing assertion and serial execution while discarding the ordinary suite’s heap, timers, streams, globals, and handles before each browser gate.

### Alternative design: add `--isolate`

Add `--isolate` to `package.json:23`.

Trade-offs:

- Smaller textual change.
- Addresses cross-file globals and leaked handles.
- Does not provide as strong an OS-process/heap boundary as separate invocations.
- Makes diagnosis harder because browser failures remain buried inside the 69-file run.

### Alternative design: browser-lifecycle refactor

Replace WP3’s manual Chrome spawn/CDP/process tracking with the existing Playwright `launchPersistentContext()` pattern used in `scripts/verify-browser-runtime.ts:400`.

Trade-offs:

- Removes duplicated Chrome lifecycle machinery and the remote-debugging-port allocation.
- Better direct fix for WP3 shutdown.
- Does not address the alternating WP4 full-suite failure.
- Higher migration risk than changing the test invocation boundary.

**Recommendation:** split the two wrappers into fresh invocations. Also harden WP3 teardown separately so a graceful-exit timeout escalates to Windows process-tree termination and cleanup continues. Do not extend timeouts or retry failed tests.

## Deterministic verification

After applying the split, run the ordinary prefix once and each browser gate three times in fresh processes:

```bash
mapfile -t core_tests < <(
  find apps packages scripts services tests -type f \
    \( -name '*.test.ts' -o -name '*.test.tsx' \) \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts' \
    ! -path 'tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts' |
  sort
)

bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 "${core_tests[@]}" &&
for run in 1 2 3; do
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts &&
  bun test --max-concurrency 1 --timeout 30000 tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts ||
  exit 1
done
```

This is repetition for verification, not a retry-based production fix. No files were modified and no additional full suite was run."

result:"I read this as a read-only leak investigation - I traced cross-file state and browser/process teardown and identified the safest isolation boundary.

## Conclusion

The exact full-suite root cause is **inconclusive** because WP4’s failure assertion was unavailable. I found no persistent profile, service-worker, port, or Chrome leak that explains both failures.

The strongest explanation is **resource/handle accumulation in the long-lived, non-isolated Bun test process combined with fragile browser teardown deadlines**. The browser harnesses themselves already run in fresh Node subprocesses, so isolating their Bun wrapper files from the other 67 files is the lowest-risk deterministic fix.

## Concrete findings

- `package.json:23` runs all 69 files in one Bun process without `--isolate`.
- Bun 1.3.14 explicitly provides `--isolate` so leaked globals and handles from one test file cannot affect another.

Specific cleanup defects can accumulate before the browser gates:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` and `:192` open SSE response bodies but never consume or cancel them. Service processes are killed in `afterEach`, but the parent-side fetch streams are not explicitly released.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls asynchronous `server.stop(true)` without awaiting it.
- Several successful waits create uncancellable `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers. Most are bounded to 2–10 seconds, so they are real transient retention rather than a convincing multi-minute root cause:
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`
  - `apps/stage/src/App.test.tsx:57,70`

WP3 teardown has a more serious failure-path flaw:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-984` waits only five seconds for natural Chrome exit.
- If that deadline expires at `:975`, execution skips service termination and profile cleanup at `:984-987`.
- Thus the reported “Chrome process exit timeout” is primarily a brittle cleanup assertion; once triggered, it also creates an actual process/resource leak.
- CDP disconnect and OS process exit are separate events. Under complete-suite pressure, Chrome can disconnect correctly but take over five seconds for its process tree to terminate.

WP4’s harness is cleaner:

- It uses Playwright-owned `chromium.launch()` and `browser.close()` at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:888`.
- Its module-level `process.on("unhandledRejection")` at `:3` is never removed, but this module runs in a one-shot Node subprocess, so it cannot accumulate across the 69 Bun files.
- Profiles and service workers are not shared: WP3 uses a PID-qualified clean profile; WP4 uses ephemeral browser contexts.

Happy DOM is not the primary leak:

- Registrations in the React tests pair `GlobalRegistrator.register()` with an awaited Promise-returning `afterAll(() => GlobalRegistrator.unregister())`.
- `tests/setup.ts` is no longer a Bun preload; it is imported only by `UpdateCoordinator.test.ts`.
- Some tests leave window listeners attached, but unregistering Happy DOM closes that window after the file.

## Lowest-risk deterministic change

Split the heavyweight browser wrappers into fresh Bun invocations:

1. Run the ordinary suite while excluding:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Run WP3 in a fresh Bun process.
3. Run WP4 in another fresh Bun process.

This preserves every assertion, remains sequential, and introduces no sleeps, retries, skips, or weaker deadlines. It is stronger than merely adding `--isolate`, because each browser gate receives a fresh OS process and heap.

Secondarily, harden WP3 cleanup by using Playwright-owned `launchPersistentContext()` or by force-terminating and awaiting the Chrome process tree after CDP shutdown instead of failing before the remaining cleanup executes.

## Inspection performed

Reviewed package/Bun configuration, all browser wrappers and harnesses, process-spawning E2E tests, model-isolate lifecycle, Bun servers, SSE/WebSocket readers, Happy DOM registration, global mutations, AbortSignal timers, profile/artifact paths, and relevant cleanup history. I ran only static searches, process inspection, and `bun test --help`; no full or browser suite was run."

- Thus the reported “Chrome process exit timeout” is primarily a brittle cleanup assertion; once triggered, it also creates an actual process/resource leak.
- CDP disconnect and OS process exit are separate events. Under complete-suite pressure, Chrome can disconnect correctly but take over five seconds for its process tree to terminate.

WP4’s harness is cleaner:

- It uses Playwright-owned `chromium.launch()` and `browser.close()` at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:888`.
- Its module-level `process.on("unhandledRejection")` at `:3` is never removed, but this module runs in a one-shot Node subprocess, so it cannot accumulate across the 69 Bun files.
- Profiles and service workers are not shared: WP3 uses a PID-qualified clean profile; WP4 uses ephemeral browser contexts.

Happy DOM is not the primary leak:

- Registrations in the React tests pair `GlobalRegistrator.register()` with an awaited Promise-returning `afterAll(() => GlobalRegistrator.unregister())`.
- `tests/setup.ts` is no longer a Bun preload; it is imported only by `UpdateCoordinator.test.ts`.
- Some tests leave window listeners attached, but unregistering Happy DOM closes that window after the file.

## Lowest-risk deterministic change

Split the heavyweight browser wrappers into fresh Bun invocations:

1. Run the ordinary suite while excluding:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Run WP3 in a fresh Bun process.
3. Run WP4 in another fresh Bun process.

This preserves every assertion, remains sequential, and introduces no sleeps, retries, skips, or weaker deadlines. It is stronger than merely adding `--isolate`, because each browser gate receives a fresh OS process and heap.

Secondarily, harden WP3 cleanup by using Playwright-owned `launchPersistentContext()` or by force-terminating and awaiting the Chrome process tree after CDP shutdown instead of failing before the remaining cleanup executes.

## ROOT CAUSE

### 1. Most likely: long-lived Bun-suite resource/handle accumulation reaches timing-sensitive browser subprocesses

The browser behavior itself is not sequence-dependent:

- WP3 passes alone.
- WP4 passes alone.
- The exact WP3 -> soak -> WP4 sequence passes.
- The failing browser alternates between full runs.

That rules against shared browser profiles, fixed E2E ordering, and direct WP3-to-WP4 contamination. The material difference is the preceding 66 test files sharing one Bun process.

Architecture:

1. `package.json:23` runs every test file in one non-isolated Bun invocation.
2. WP3 and WP4 wrappers spawn one-shot Node verifiers:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts:41`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts:50`
3. Those Node processes own Chrome and services; earlier test modules cannot directly mutate their module state. They can, however, leave the Bun parent with memory, timers, streams, sockets, or OS pressure while it waits for them.

WP4 is explicitly wall-clock sensitive:

- Event waits default to 30 seconds: `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:265`
- Recovery duration uses `performance.now()`: `:596-601`
- Any recovery over 30 seconds becomes a gate failure: `:602`
- The verifier rejects the aggregate: `scripts/verify-wp4-topology-e2e.ts:11-18`

Normal WP4 took 65.84 seconds; failed WP4 took 142.04 seconds. The additional approximately 76 seconds is consistent with delayed browser/event processing or multiple recovery deadlines, not deterministic state corruption.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The missing WP4 assertion prevents proving whether it was a recovery deadline, event timeout, or teardown failure.

### 2. Confirmed amplifier: WP3 cleanup turns delayed Chrome exit into a failure and then skips all remaining cleanup

WP3 first closes the context and sends `Browser.close`:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-958`

It then allows only five seconds for OS process exit:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:967-979`

If that deadline expires at `:975`, the exception aborts the `finally` block before:

- Remaining services are terminated: `:984`
- Profile and snapshots are removed: `:985-987`

Therefore, `Chrome process exit timeout` does not establish a failed browser scenario. It says the E2E completed but Chrome did not finish OS-level teardown within five seconds. Under resource pressure, the cleanup assertion becomes the test failure and creates the leak it was intended to detect.

WP3 also launches bare Chrome manually with a persistent profile and CDP port at `:471-488`, unlike WP4’s Playwright-owned launch at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:798`. That increases lifecycle code and shutdown states owned by the harness.

**Confidence: high for the reported WP3 failure and cleanup leak; it does not alone explain WP4.**

### 3. Lower-ranked contributor: earlier successful tests retain parent-side handles briefly

Concrete examples:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` opens an SSE response without consuming or cancelling its body.
- The same occurs for controller events at `:192`.
- Cleanup kills services at `:11-16`, but does not explicitly release those response bodies.

## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). Default configstore is `FileConfigstore` ([index.ts#L32-L46](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L32-L46)), which is just `FileKvStore` re-exported ([configstores/index.ts](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/configstores/index.ts)) — it writes `<id>.json` next to the upload: `await fs.writeFile(this.resolve(key), JSON.stringify(value))` ([FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12), [FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31)).
- **Write (PATCH)**: opens the same file with `fs.createWriteStream(file_path, { flags: 'r+', start: offset })` — appends at the exact client-reported offset — counts bytes through a transform, and returns the new `offset + bytes_received` ([index.ts#L97-L128](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L97-L128)).
- **Read (HEAD/resume)**: `getUpload` does NOT trust any in-memory counter. It re-reads the JSON info file for `size`/`metadata`/`creation_date` and then **`offset: stats.size`** — the actual byte length from `fs.stat` ([index.ts#L130-L165](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L130-L165)). So the source of truth for the resume offset is the persisted file itself; a process restart loses nothing.
- This "file + adjacent info file" layout is documented as the universal store pattern: *"All stores (as in the `datastore` option) save two files, the uploaded file and an info file with metadata, usually adjacent to each other"* ([server README, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).

### Where memory is used (and isn't)

- The default **locker** is `MemoryLocker` — `locks = new Map<string, LockEntry>()` in-process ([MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/lockers/MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34)); README says explicitly: *"By default it uses an in-memory locker... When running multiple instances of the server, you need to provide a locker implementation that is shared between all instances (such as a `RedisLocker`)"* ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- In-memory KV stores (`MemoryKvStore`, re-exported as `MemoryConfigstore`) exist but are intended as caches for cloud stores (e.g. `@tus/s3-store` `cache:` option) — the README's KV-store section only shows `MemoryKvStore` used as an S3 metadata cache, never as the source of truth ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- Conclusion for the report: **persisted** for FileStore (offset = file size on disk, metadata = JSON sidecar); **in-memory only** for the default lock and for optional cloud-store caches.
